query: For an equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy made from low-activation refractory elements, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains its plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading relevant to sustained plasma-facing-component service? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations expected relative to pure tungsten, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The enhanced high-temperature ductility and toughness of the equimolar WTaTiVZr HEA relative to pure W under plasma‐facing service conditions arises from multicomponent lattice distortion–driven solid‐solution strengthening, which raises the lattice friction stress and promotes delocalized, cross‐slip–mediated plasticity, thereby suppressing brittle cleavage and elevating uniform elongation and fracture toughness at 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar WTaTiVZr high‐entropy alloy and commercially pure tungsten, both processed to an average grain size of ~5 μm via identical thermomechanical schedules.
generation.intervention: Replacing pure W with the equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy in high‐temperature tensile and fracture tests.
generation.conditions: Uniaxial tensile and single-edge-notch‐bend (SENB) fracture toughness tests at 1000 °C in vacuum, strain rate 1×10^–3 s^–1, grain size 5±1 μm.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased lattice friction stress from multicomponent distortion and associated high dislocation density enabling cross slip and delocalized plastic flow.
generation.mechanism: Lattice distortion from multiple principal elements increases the critical stress for dislocation glide, promoting dislocation storage and cross‐slip; this distributes strain more homogeneously, reducing stress concentrations at crack tips and delaying brittle fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: At 1000 °C, the HEA will exhibit ≥50% higher uniform elongation and ≥30% higher fracture toughness (K_IC) than pure W.
generation.baseline: Pure W at 1000 °C: uniform elongation ~1% and fracture toughness ~10 MPa·√m under the same test conditions.
generation.boundary: Valid for temperatures 900–1100 °C, strain rates 1×10^–4–1×10^–2 s^–1, vacuum environment, grain sizes 3–7 μm.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate; extension from room‐temperature data to sustained high‐temperature loading; limited existing high‐T data on this specific HEA.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce W and WTaTiVZr specimens with identical (~5 μm) grain sizes. Conduct uniaxial tensile tests and SENB fracture toughness tests at 1000 °C in vacuum, strain rate 1×10^–3 s^–1. Measure uniform elongation and K_IC under identical loading and specimen geometry.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not show ≥50% increase in uniform elongation and ≥30% increase in K_IC compared to pure W under the specified conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.
